h1:
Kanchanaburi with Kids: 3 Days, 2 Nights
Waterfalls, Raft Houses, the Train
intro: You can have a great time in Kanchanaburi with kids without hard jungle hikes or cramming in so many stops that everyone melts down. The trick is to pick activities where kids get to swim, ride a real train, and sleep somewhere new like a raft house on the river. This plan spreads it over three days with built-in breaks: day one is checking into the raft house and letting the kids settle in by the water, day two goes all-in on Erawan Falls in the morning when the water is clear and the crowds are thin, and the last day is a short ride on the Death Railway before the drive home. We've packed in the timing, entry fees, what you should bring, and the spots where parents need to keep a close eye on the little ones.

blocks.html: Kanchanaburi works well for families because the attractions are clustered fairly close together, and there's water to swim in, accommodation that gets kids excited, and a train you can actually ride. The one real challenge is distance: Erawan Falls sits about 65 km north of the town. So we base the family at a raft house in an easy-to-reach zone, then make day trips out from there. Driving yourself is the smoothest option because you'll have a lot of kid gear to haul, but if you don't have a car you can take the local train on the Bridge–Tham Krasae stretch and hire a vehicle out to Erawan.

blocks.text: Overview, budget, and what to pack

blocks.html: These three days are relaxed and unhurried, with time built in for naps and snacking along the way. The things to plan ahead are booking the raft house — especially on long weekends, when they fill up fast — and the local train schedule, which only runs a few times a day. Erawan Falls entry for Thais is 60 THB for adults and 30 THB for children, plus 30 THB per car.

items: Length — 3 days, 2 nights. Leave Bangkok early on day one; it's about a 2.5-hour drive to the town.
Getting around — driving yourself is easiest because of all the kid gear. Without a car, take the local train on the Bridge–Tham Krasae stretch, then hire a songthaew out to Erawan.
Rough budget per family — entry fees and tickets add up to only a couple hundred baht total. Raft houses start around 800–2,000 THB/night for in-town ones; food depends on your style.
What to pack for the kids — life jackets or floaties, non-slip water shoes, sunscreen, mosquito repellent, a change of clothes, and snacks to head off meltdowns on the road.

blocks.title: Book the activities in your Kanchanaburi trip ahead
blocks.text: Booking online ahead on Klook or GetYourGuide is usually cheaper than the gate and skips the queue. Pick only the experiences you actually want — prices and availability are shown live on each site.

items.label: Day trips from Kanchanaburi
items.note: Out and back in a day

blocks.text: Day 1 — Arrive, check into the raft house, let the kids settle by the water

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Travel · Raft check-in · Splashing around the raft

items.activity: Leave Bangkok early, with a bathroom break on the way
items.note: It's about a 2.5-hour drive. With young kids, stop at a gas station once to stretch their legs and use the toilet. Keep snacks in the car so they don't get bored.

items.activity: Reach the town and have lunch at a riverside spot near the bridge
items.note: There are several riverside restaurants around here serving local dishes or river fish. Pick one with enough room for a stroller or that has high chairs.

items.activity: Check into a raft house on the River Kwai
items.note: Go for an in-town raft house — it's easier to reach, cheaper, and tends to have proper guard rails. Ask ahead whether they lend out children's life jackets. The wilderness raft houses out toward Sai Yok have a more natural feel, but some require a boat to reach and have limited electricity, which can be awkward with young kids.

items.activity: Let the kids splash by the raft or sit at the water's edge
items.note: The River Kwai flows and runs deep, so kids need life jackets and an adult watching closely at all times. Never let a child into the water alone. Many raft houses have a shallow zone or a separate pool that's safer — stick to those.

items.activity: Watch the sunset and have dinner by the river
items.note: Many raft houses have their own dining room; order ahead so you're not waiting long. If you're staying in town, finding a place outside is easy too. The riverside gets breezy at night, so bring a light jacket for the kids.

blocks.title: Water and kids: be careful
blocks.html: The River Kwai has currents and deep spots, so don't get complacent even if your child can swim. Put a life jacket on them every time they're near the water or out on the raft deck, and have one adult whose only job is watching the kids — not scrolling on a phone. At night, close or block off the way down to the water before the kids go to bed.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Erawan Falls, a full day of swimming

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Erawan National Park · Swimming · Back to the raft house

items.activity: Have breakfast at the raft house, then head out to Erawan
items.note: From town it's about 65 km north, roughly an hour and a half. Going early means easy parking, clearer water, and cooler air that's easier on the kids' legs.

items.activity: Arrive at the park and walk up to swim at the lower tiers
items.note: The park is open roughly 07:00–16:30. Entry for Thais is 60 THB for adults, 30 THB for children, and 30 THB per car. The falls have 7 tiers; tiers 1–2 have easy paths and are great for kids to swim, with little fish that nibble your feet — a thrill for kids. Wear non-slip water shoes because the rocks are slippery.

items.activity: Lay out a mat, have a snack, take turns in the water
items.note: Find a shady spot beside one of the tiers and set up a mat as your base. Take turns watching the gear and watching the kids. Let little ones play in the shallow pools with their life jackets on. You can't carry plastic bottles above a certain tier — there's a bottle-deposit point for that.

items.activity: Come down from the falls, rinse off, change clothes, have lunch
items.note: From tier 3 up, the path gets steep and turns into rocks and tree roots. With young kids there's no need to push for all 7 tiers — the lower ones are plenty of fun. There are restaurants and showers near the park entrance, at tourist-spot prices.

items.activity: Drive back to the raft house and let the kids nap in the car
items.note: After a morning of swimming, kids usually fall asleep in the car right on cue. You'll get back to the raft house in the late afternoon — let the kids rest before dinner. No need to add another stop today.

blocks.title: Don't force all 7 tiers
blocks.html: For kids, Erawan's charm is the lower tiers, where the swimming is easy and the fish nibble. There's no need to drag them all the way up to tier 7, where the upper path is steep and slippery and the risk of falling is real. Enjoy tiers 1–4 to the fullest, then head back down to rest — everyone has fun and nobody melts down.

blocks.text: Day 3 — Ride the Death Railway, then drive home

blocks.label: Day 3
blocks.title: Bridge over the River Kwai · Death Railway · Journey home

items.activity: Pack up, check out, and head to the Bridge over the River Kwai
items.note: You can walk across the roughly 300-meter steel bridge for free. Hold the kids' hands tight, because there are gaps between the sleepers and no guard rail along the way. There are pull-out spots at intervals in case a train passes. Go early while the sun is still mild.

items.activity: Board the Death Railway at River Kwai Bridge station for a short ride
items.note: The local train only runs a few times a day; third-class tickets cost a few tens of baht. Most kids are thrilled to ride a real train. On the Tham Krasae curve, the train runs along the cliff face beside the Khwae Noi river — a lovely view. Put the kids on the window side and hold onto them when the train sways.

items.activity: Get off at Tham Krasae, walk the wooden trestle, take photos
items.note: If you drove, park the car, buy tickets for the short ride, then either drive on to pick everyone up at the next station. The cliffside stretch gets crowded and the wooden walkway is narrow, so keep the kids on the inside and watch the edge.

items.activity: Have lunch and stop for souvenirs in town
items.note: Stop at a souvenir shop for thong muan (crispy rolled wafers), kon thong, or seasonal fruit. Have a filling lunch before the long drive.

You'll reach Bangkok right around evening. If you're heading back on a Sunday, leaving in the early afternoon helps you dodge the return traffic. Pack snacks and a pillow so the kids can rest in the car.

blocks.text: Adjusting the plan for your kids' ages

items.name: With preschoolers
items.blurb: Skip the upper-tier waterfall walk and focus on the lower tiers and the raft house pool. Add more nap time, and pick an in-town raft house with guard rails and shallow water.

items.name: With older grade-schoolers
items.blurb: You can add more challenge: walk up several tiers at Erawan, try kayaking on a calm stretch, or stop by the war museum so the kids learn some history.

items.name: No private car
items.blurb: Stay at an in-town raft house within walking distance of the bridge and train station. Take the local train on the Bridge–Tham Krasae stretch, then hire a songthaew or join a tour out to Erawan on day two.

blocks.title: Book the raft house ahead and pick a kid-safe one
blocks.html: On long weekends and during the cool season, River Kwai raft houses fill up very fast. If you're traveling with kids, ask before booking whether the raft has guard rails around the deck, whether they lend children's life jackets, and whether there's a shallow zone or a separate pool. Wilderness raft houses that require a boat to reach and have limited electricity may not be convenient for young kids — choose based on your children's ages.

faq.q: How many days should we spend in Kanchanaburi with young kids?
faq.a: Three days and two nights is about right for a family with young kids, because it leaves room for them to rest and nap without cramming in so much that they melt down. If your kids are still very small or tire easily, you can trim it to 2 days and 1 night and focus on just the raft house and the falls.

faq.q: Is Erawan Falls good for kids to swim in?
faq.a: Yes, especially tiers 1–2, where the paths are easy and there are shallow pools for kids to play in, plus little fish that nibble their feet for a thrill. But wear non-slip water shoes because the rocks are slippery, put life jackets on younger kids, and keep an adult close. Don't force young kids up the upper tiers, where the path is steep and slippery.

faq.q: Is sleeping on a raft house safe with kids?
faq.a: It's safe if you choose a raft house with guard rails around the deck and a way to block off the path down to the water. Put a life jacket on the kids whenever they're near the water, have an adult watching at all times, and never let a child into the water alone. At night, close or block off the way down before the kids go to bed. Many raft houses have a shallow zone or separate pool that's safer than the river.

faq.q: How much is Erawan Falls entry for children?
faq.a: For Thais, children's entry is 30 THB, adults 60 THB, plus 30 THB per car. The park is open roughly 07:00–16:30. These prices can change, so check again before you go.

faq.q: Which stretch of the Death Railway should we ride with kids?
faq.a: We recommend the short stretch from River Kwai Bridge station down to Tham Krasae. It doesn't take so long that the kids get bored, and you see the most beautiful cliffside section along the river. Put the kids on the window side and hold onto them when the train sways. Check the train times with the station or the SRT hotline 1690 beforehand, since it only runs a few times a day.
